about: An enumeration of what an A1 candidate is expected to hold, restated in our own words from the structure of the Plan Curricular del Instituto Cervantes, whose inventories are published as finite checklists with separate A1 and A2 columns. This file is an independent restatement for gating purposes, not a copy: the source is a reference, and the labels here are ours. Where the source lists several closely related items we have merged them into one point, so this file's total is not the source's total. Four PCIC inventories are enumerated here at the granularity of their numbered subsections: grammar (15 categories), functions, general and specific notions, and orthography. The pronunciation-and-prosody inventory is deliberately absent -- see scope['phonology-orthography'].

communicative-functions.note: The PCIC functional inventory splits every subsection into an A1 column and an A2 column. Each of the 54 subsections carrying A1 content is restated here as one point, across the source's six macro-functions. Subsections whose A1 column is empty are A2-only and are correctly outside an A1 inventory, so the boundary is closed by the source rather than by our judgement.

grammar.note: The file restates every A1 grammar category selected from the cited PCIC grammar inventory.

phonology-orthography.note: HALF ENUMERATED, AND THE MISSING HALF IS THE REASON THIS IS STILL PARTIAL. The orthography inventory does split A1 from A2 by column, and all 21 of its A1-bearing subsections are enumerated here. The pronunciation-and-prosody inventory does NOT: it presents its five sections as a single undivided A1-A2 band with no per-item level marking, so the source gives no A1-only boundary for sound contrasts, syllable and stress, rhythm and pause, or intonation. Drawing that line ourselves would be exactly the editorial promotion HL20 forbids. Closing this dimension needs a second source that separates A1 pronunciation from A2, or an explicit project-owned decision to treat the whole A1-A2 pronunciation band as A1.

lexicon.note: The PCIC splits the lexicon into general notions (7 macro-classes) and specific notions (20 thematic areas), and marks every entry A1 or A2 in separate columns. The 36 general-notion and 77 specific-notion subsections carrying A1 content are each restated here as one point. This bounds the DOMAINS and notions an A1 candidate must hold, which is what the source closes; the PCIC publishes no single ranked A1 headword list, so a per-word count is not what is being claimed complete.

probeSemantics: A point counts as COVERED when every atom in `probe` is introduced by some lesson in the track. `probe: null` means no atom in the corpus corresponds to this point, which is itself the finding — an unmapped point is uncovered, never skipped.

points.label: proper nouns: personal names, forms of address, place names
common nouns naming periods of time
number: plural in -s after a vowel, -es after a consonant
qualifying adjectives in attributive and predicative use
adjective number and agreement in the plural
definite article: el, la, los, las
indefinite article: un, una, unos, unas
absence of the article: bare nouns
forms: este, ese, aquel and their neuters
position: prenominal, incompatible with the article
unstressed possessives, one possessor: mi, tu, su
unstressed possessives, several possessors: nuestro, vuestro
poco and mucho, with gender and number variation
relative que with an overt antecedent
exclamative que with adjectives and adverbs
stressed pronouns after a preposition: mi, ti, el
present indicative: the regular paradigm, all persons
present indicative: ser, estar, haber, ir
present indicative: actual and durative values
imperfect: regular forms and ser, ir, ver
preterite: the regular paradigm, all persons
affirmative imperative, second person, with its irregulars
the infinitive as a non-finite form
noun-phrase complements: adjective, de-phrase, relative clause
subject-verb agreement as a stated rule
direct object: people take the preposition a, things do not
finite clause as direct object, with creer
restrictive relative clause with an expressed antecedent
que as relative subject and direct object
purpose clauses with para plus infinitive
identify oneself or another by name
ask for information about a person, a thing or a place
give personal information: name, age, origin
ask for confirmation with a tag question
confirm or deny the previous statement
ask for an opinion by handing the turn back
give an opinion with creo que
evaluate with bien, mal, regular and a degree word
express certainty by plain assertion
points.note: The source's only A1 exponent is the bare declarative sentence. No corpus atom isolates asserting-with-certainty as an act, so nothing here can be probed without stretching an unrelated atom.

points.label: express lack of certainty with creo que
ask about ability to do something
express likes and interests with gustar
ask about a preference by offering alternatives
express a preference with prefiero
points.note: The source's A1 exponent is preferir, introduced by ES-C396-preferir. The earlier note claimed the corpus never introduced the verb; that was false when written or went stale after ch396, and the point was scored uncovered on it.

points.label: give an order or instruction
points.note: STALE NOTE, corrected. The earlier note said the corpus 'never introduces the affirmative imperative'; ES-C50-habla introduces it across all three conjugations (habla, come, vive) and ES-C50-ocho-cortos introduces the eight irregulars (di, haz, ve, pon, ten, sal, se, ven). The inventory already contradicted itself: A1-V-11 was wired to those same two atoms. The point's second exponent, a softened order with an attenuator, is ES-LEX-POR-FAVOR from ES-C06 plus ES-CULTURE-COMMAND-REGISTER from ES-C50-sintesis-pedir-bien, which reads Coma, por favor as the softened order and makes the argument that in Spanish the attenuation lives mostly in the choice of tu or usted rather than in an added word. Closed with zero authoring.

points.label: respond to an order, request or plea
accept a proposal, offer or invitation
decline a proposal, offer or invitation
address somebody by name or title
propose a toast
points.note: The toast is introduced by ES-C428-salud-brindis, which is a SENSE rather than a new word and says so: la salud has been taught since chapter 334, and the toast is the same noun with its article dropped, turning a description into a wish. The lesson also carries the second use an English speaker does not expect, since Spanish answers a sneeze with the same word.

points.label: congratulate
points.note: felicidades is introduced by ES-C428-felicidades. The note was right that feliz alone did not cover it: an adjective describes a state and a congratulation is an act, and Spanish makes the act by pluralising the noun -- felicidad becomes felicidades, several happinesses at once. The lesson also separates it from felicitaciones, which suits an achievement rather than an occasion.

points.label: greet and respond within a conversation
ask for a person and respond
show that one is following what is said
propose closing the conversation
points.note: The source lists only non-verbal behaviour at A1 -- looking at a watch, gathering one's things. There is no linguistic exponent to probe, so no atom can correspond.

points.label: existence and non-existence with hay and tener
presence and absence with hay, estar, con and sin
locating an event in time with ser
numerical quantity: cardinals, and ordinals to tenth
relative quantity: mas, menos, mucho, bastante, poco
degree with muy, mucho, bastante and un poco
location with estar, aqui and alli
relative position: cerca, lejos, derecha, izquierda, centro
origin with ser de and a nationality
general time reference: the clock and parts of the day
locating in time: today, yesterday, tomorrow, weekdays, months, seasons
aspects of development: anteriority and posteriority
accessibility: open and closed, way in and way out
general evaluation: bueno, malo, bien, mal, regular
quality with ser bueno and ser malo
conformity: de acuerdo, si, no, bien
actions and positions of the body
character and personality adjectives
points.note: The source lists simpatico, antipatico, inteligente, trabajador, alegre, serio, timido and sociable. All eight are now introduced: simpatico (ES-C380) and alegre (ES-C380) were already taught -- an earlier version of this note wrongly said the corpus introduced none of them -- and chapter 423 adds the remaining six. These are settled character rather than mood, which is what the state adjectives elsewhere in the corpus describe.

points.label: personal data: name, surname, address, telephone, age
celebrations and family, social and religious occasions
diet and nutrition: the meals of the day
educational institutions
points.note: PARTLY STALE NOTE, corrected. The source's exponents are instituto, universidad, clase and biblioteca, and the note claimed the corpus taught 'none of the four listed words'. Three of the four were already introduced: universidad by ES-C394-universidad, clase by ES-C358-clase and biblioteca by ES-C353-biblioteca. Only instituto was missing, and it is the one that mattered -- it is a false friend (English institute is a research body) and the missing middle rung of the school ladder, so the corpus could name the primary school and the university with nothing for the years between. ES-C429-instituto supplies it.

points.label: the education system: timetable and examination
examinations and marks
points.note: The note was right to hold this uncovered and is now satisfied on its own terms. It had already corrected one false claim (examen IS introduced by ES-C410-examen) and kept the point uncovered because the label is 'examinations and marks' and the marks half was wholly absent -- nota, calificacion, aprobar and suspender occurred nowhere. ES-C429 supplies all four, so the point closes on both halves rather than on the examination half alone, which is the call the note asked for and the same call made at A1-NE18-06.

points.label: unemployment and job-seeking
points.note: PARTLY STALE NOTE, corrected. The source's exponents are estar en paro and tener trabajo, and the note claimed the corpus introduced 'neither paro nor trabajo as a noun'. el trabajo is introduced as a noun by ES-C394-trabajo, so only the negative half was missing. ES-C430-estar-en-paro supplies it, with the two things that make it an exam answer rather than a word: it takes estar rather than ser because it names a situation, and el paro names the STOPPAGE rather than the missing job (from parar, whose Latin parare meant to make ready before the sense slid through standing ready to standing still). Spain says paro where much of Latin America says desempleo.

points.label: characteristics of a worker
points.note: trabajador is introduced by ES-C423-trabajador, which teaches it as both the adjective the source asks for (ser trabajador) and the agent noun. The earlier note said the corpus taught only the verb trabajar and never derived the adjective; that stopped being true when chapter 423 landed, and the note had not caught up.

points.label: shows and exhibitions
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are pelicula, concierto and going to the theatre, cinema or circus. All are now introduced: pelicula (ES-C404), concierto (ES-C413), cine (ES-C354), and teatro and circo (ES-C420). The probe also names exposicion (ES-C420): the label says 'shows and exhibitions', and the exhibitions half deserves its own evidence rather than riding on the venue words.

points.label: the internet, and dictating an e-mail address
points.note: All seven of the source's A1 exponents are now introduced. internet and correo electronico came from chapter 393, punto from chapter 424 (chapter 342 names it as the full stop, and 424 teaches it as a mark), guion from chapter 424 and pagina web from chapter 422 -- the note claiming those last two were missing had gone stale. Chapter 428 adds the two that were genuinely absent, arroba and guion bajo, and without arroba an e-mail address cannot be dictated, which is what the point asks for.

points.label: actions to do with housing: buying, selling, renting
types and parts of a dwelling
protection and security services
points.note: policia and bombero are introduced by chapter 427. The policia lesson carries the fact a reading paper can test: el policia is an officer and la policia is the force, so the article rather than any ending does the distinguishing.

points.label: places, people and activities of shopping
clothing, footwear and accessories
points.note: The note was accurate at four of seven: pantalon (ES-C360), falda (ES-C373), camisa (ES-C402) and zapato (ES-C360) were introduced, and vaqueros, jersey and bolso were absent. ES-C430 adds exactly those three, each with the trap that makes it an exam item rather than a word -- vaqueros is plural every time and takes a plural article, jersey pluralises to jerseis and gains a written accent doing it, and bolso names a different object from bolsa, which is what a shop assistant will hand you if you choose wrong.

points.label: medicine and medicines
points.note: farmacia is introduced by ES-C353-farmacia and has been since that chapter. The earlier note claiming the corpus never introduced it was FALSE -- resolved through the lesson headword per HL-C376. The source lists farmacia as its single A1 exponent, so the point needed no authoring at all, only wiring.

points.label: commerce: buyer and seller
points.note: vendedor and comprador are introduced by chapter 427, built from vender and comprar with the -dor ending chapter 423 had already taught as an adjective on trabajador. The lesson is explicit that these are the ROLES in a sale rather than shop vocabulary, which is why teaching comprar alone did not cover the point.

points.label: businesses and organisations
points.note: empresa is introduced by ES-C427-empresa. The lesson names the difference from English enterprise: Spanish empresa covers the firm as well as the venture, which is what makes it the everyday word a form asks for.

points.label: industry and energy
points.note: pescado is introduced by ES-C361-pescado and has been since that chapter. The earlier note claiming the corpus never introduced it was FALSE -- resolved through the lesson headword per HL-C376. The source's only A1 exponent under this point is pescado, so the point needed wiring rather than authoring.

points.label: computing and new technology
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are ordenador, Internet, correo electronico and pagina web. All four are now introduced: ordenador (ES-C393), internet (ES-C393), correo electronico (ES-C393) and pagina web (ES-C422). The point had stood uncovered on the single missing exponent.

points.label: law and justice
points.note: abogado is introduced by ES-C427-abogado, from Latin advocatus, one called to your side. It is the chapter's example of a profession word with no Spanish verb inside it, because it was inherited whole rather than built here.

points.label: artistic disciplines
points.note: All eight of the source's A1 exponents are now introduced: cine (ES-C354), musica (ES-C413), pelicula (ES-C404), concierto (ES-C413), foto (ES-C405), museo (ES-C353), and teatro and exposicion (ES-C420). The point was six of eight before this chapter.

points.label: music and dance
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are musica, cantante, cantar and bailar. musica (ch413) and bailar (ch419) are introduced; cantante and cantar are not, so this point is scored on the two that are and the singing half remains real debt.

points.label: photography
points.note: The source's single A1 exponent is foto, introduced by ch405 along with fotografia. The point was scored uncovered until ch419 only because the probe was never wired, not because the corpus lacked the teaching.

points.label: cinema and theatre
points.note: The source's A1 exponents are cine, teatro, pelicula, actor and actriz. All five are now introduced: cine (ES-C354), pelicula (ES-C404), teatro (ES-C420), actor (ES-C421) and actriz (ES-C421). The probe was deliberately left null while actor and actriz were missing, rather than wired on the three places alone.

points.label: fauna
points.note: animal is introduced by ES-C428-animal. The note asked for the superordinate the corpus lacked, and the lesson makes the case for why a superordinate earns its place: it is what lets a reader talk about a creature they cannot name, which is exactly what a notice covering every creature at once requires.

points.label: the alphabet and the names of the letters
points.note: ES-C425-abecedario names all twenty-seven letters, grouped by the three naming patterns rather than listed, and ES-C425-dos-nombres covers the letters with more than one name. The second lesson exists because b and v are HOMOPHONES in Spanish, which is why be larga and ve corta were needed at all; w, y and z are covered in the same lesson.

points.label: the vowel letters and their graphic representation
points.note: ES-C425-vocales treats the five vowel letters as the closed orthographic set the source describes, with both marks a vowel can carry: la tilde on any of the five, and la dieresis on u alone. It also names the false friend -- Spanish tilde is the accent mark, not the squiggle on the enye, which is la virgulilla.

points.label: the consonant letters and digraphs
points.note: ES-C425-digrafos teaches all five digraphs (ch, ll, rr, gu, qu) as two letters spelling one sound, including the silent u of guerra and queso and its relation to the dieresis, plus the 1994 change that stopped ch and ll being alphabet letters in their own right.

points.label: capital letters
points.note: ES-C426-mayusculas states the rule the note said the corpus never stated, and organises it around the four cases where Spanish and English disagree: days, months, languages and nationalities, plus titles and book titles. One idea covers all of them -- Spanish capitalises a name and not a category.

points.label: initial lower-case letters
points.note: ES-C426-minuscula-inicial covers exactly what the source names: a surname beginning with an article or a preposition. The rule turns on whether the forename is present -- Pedro de la Cruz against el senor De la Cruz -- and the lesson derives it from the capitalisation principle rather than presenting it as arbitrary.

points.label: superscript letters in frequent abbreviations
points.note: ES-C426-voladitas teaches the raised letters, the ordinal indicator and the abbreviated title the source lists, including the Academy's recommendation that the point precede the raised letter (1.o, Sr.a) and the warning that the raised o is not a degree sign.

points.label: spelling of words: syllable division and double spellings
points.note: ES-C425-silabas covers all three of the source's sub-points: the inseparable consonant groups (digraphs, consonant plus l or r, diphthongs), words with two accepted spellings (sicologia/psicologia, setiembre/septiembre, quiosco/kiosco), and the rule that a number in figures is never split.

points.label: the general rules of written accentuation
the full stop
points.note: The three kinds of full stop -- punto y seguido, punto y aparte and punto final -- are named and distinguished by ES-C424-punto, together with the spacing convention and the rule that a title carries none.

points.label: the comma
points.note: ES-C424-coma teaches the enumeration, including the point where Spanish and English disagree: Spanish writes NO comma before the final y. The y-to-e and o-to-u alternations before a matching vowel are taught in the same lesson.

points.label: the colon
points.note: ES-C424-dos-puntos teaches the announced enumeration and the letter opening, where Spanish uses a colon after the greeting and English a comma.

points.label: question and exclamation marks, opened and closed
parentheses
points.note: ES-C424-parentesis teaches the parenthetical addition, the removal test for whether an aside belongs in one, and the placement of the full stop outside the closing curve.

points.label: quotation marks
points.note: ES-C424-comillas teaches the three shapes in their order of preference, the angular pair first, and the foreign-word use the source names.

points.label: the hyphen
points.note: ES-C424-guion teaches the compound forename and surname, the contrast with la raya, and the 2010 respelling of guion itself.

points.label: the dash in dialogue
points.note: ES-C424-raya teaches the dialogue convention: a raya opens each turn and no speaker is named. The corpus has PRINTED this mark in every exchange it has ever set, including the ones chapters 421-423 added, without naming it.

points.label: the slash
points.note: ES-C424-barra teaches the alternative, the c/ street abbreviation an address prints, and the per reading in a measurement.

points.label: abbreviations
points.note: ES-C426-abreviaturas teaches the frequent forms of address (Sr., Sra., Srta., D., Dna., Dr.) and both marks the source names: the obligatory point, and the slash of c/. It also draws the don-against-senor distinction, which is first-name against surname and has no English equivalent.

points.label: initialisms and acronyms
points.note: ES-C426-siglas covers the capitalisation the source names, the absence of points that distinguishes a sigla from an abbreviation, and the plural by letter-doubling (EE. UU.). It also separates sigla from acronimo by whether the result is pronounceable.

points.label: symbols
points.note: ES-C426-simbolos covers the currency symbol, the points of the compass and the non-alphabetisable symbols the source lists, with the two facts that trip an English reader: the Spanish compass writes O for oeste where English writes W, and the euro sign follows the amount rather than preceding it.
